nameStory: The name 'brevis' comes from Latin meaning 'short' or 'brief,' likely referring to this spider's compact size or short legs compared to its relatives. While it doesn't have a widely-used common name, cicurinid spiders are sometimes called 'mesh web weavers' for their distinctive web style.
description: Cicurina brevis is a small, inconspicuous spider that belongs to the mesh web weaver family. These spiders are typically pale brown to grayish in color with a compact body design. They're quite small, making them easy to overlook as they go about their business in leaf litter and under logs. Like other cicurinids, they create sheet-like webs rather than the classic orb webs many people picture when thinking of spiders.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Creates small, flat sheet webs that feel slightly sticky but not gummy like orb webs, often found stretched between leaves or debris

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact, somewhat flattened appearance with relatively short legs that feel sturdy rather than delicate when gently touched

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Very small spider, easily fitting on your fingernail with room to spare

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Pale brown to grayish coloration with subtle darker markings that may appear as faint chevrons or spots

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often found hiding under objects during the day, moves quickly when disturbed with a characteristic scurrying motion

habitat: Look for these tiny spiders in moist leaf litter, under fallen logs, and in the spaces between rocks where organic matter accumulates. They prefer areas with good moisture retention and plenty of small hiding spots. In New England, they're most likely found in deciduous and mixed forests where decomposing leaves create the humid microhabitats they need.

seasonality.spring: Adults become more active as temperatures warm, beginning to establish territories and build their characteristic sheet webs.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most easily observed, though they remain quite secretive during daylight hours.
seasonality.fall: Mating season occurs, with spiders preparing for winter by seeking sheltered overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Remarkably, recent research shows this species is actually more active under snow cover than in summer, thriving in the insulated subnivium layer.

funFact: This little spider has a secret winter life! Scientists recently discovered that Cicurina brevis is actually MORE active under the snowpack in winter than during summer, living it up in the cozy 'subnivium' - the insulated space between snow and ground where temperatures stay around freezing even when it's frigid above.
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small ground-dwelling spiders, but the distinctive flat sheet web is the giveaway - if you see tiny mesh-like webs in leaf litter rather than funnel webs or no webs at all, you're likely looking at a cicurinid.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'subnivium' refers to the special ecosystem that exists in the layer between snow and ground during winter - it's like a hidden world where many creatures remain active while we assume everything is dormant above.
compareHints: Cicurina brevis is distinguished from its relatives like C. pallida and C. robusta primarily by its smaller size and more compact build. While all cicurinids make similar sheet webs, C. brevis tends to build smaller, more delicate versions. Its remarkable winter activity under snow may also be a unique trait, though this behavior hasn't been extensively studied in its relatives yet.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to other Cicurina species that might occur in New England, the pale cicurina lives up to its name with notably lighter coloration than its relatives.
